blocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
AML/CFT Compliance in UAE — Common Questions
Questions commonly asked by DNFBPs and regulated entities about AML/CFT/CPF compliance obligations in the UAE.

items.q: What is AML/CFT compliance and who does it apply to in the UAE?

a.text: Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Counter-Terrorist Financing (CFT) compliance refers to the set of legal obligations designed to prevent the use of financial systems for money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing. In the UAE, these obligations apply to financial institutions — including banks, insurance companies, investment firms, and securities participants — as well as Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions (DNFBPs) such as real estate brokers, corporate service providers, auditors, and dealers in precious metals and stones. The primary legal framework is Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 and its Executive Regulations under Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025.

items.q: Who qualifies as a DNFBP under UAE AML law?

a.text: Under the UAE AML framework, Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions (DNFBPs) include real estate brokers and developers, dealers in precious metals and stones (DPMS), corporate service providers and company formation agents, auditors and accounting firms, lawyers and legal advisors engaged in specific financial transactions, and other non-financial businesses designated by the relevant supervisory authority. DNFBPs are supervised primarily by the Ministry of Economy and are subject to risk-based AML/CFT/CPF obligations proportionate to the nature and complexity of their activities.

items.q: What is Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 and what does it change?

a.text: Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 on Combating Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and the Financing of Proliferation is the current governing AML/CFT law in the UAE. It repeals and replaces Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 and introduces strengthened risk-based obligations for both financial institutions and DNFBPs. Its Executive Regulations are set out under Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025. Key obligations include enterprise-wide risk assessments, customer due diligence, UBO transparency, targeted financial sanctions screening, and STR filing with the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit via the goAML system.

items.q: Is an Enterprise-Wide Risk Assessment (EWRA) mandatory for DNFBPs in the UAE?

a.text: Yes. Under the UAE AML framework, DNFBPs are required to conduct and document an Enterprise-Wide Risk Assessment (EWRA) that evaluates AML/CFT/CPF risks across customer types, products and services, geographies, delivery channels, and transaction profiles. The EWRA must be risk-based, documented, and updated periodically — particularly when there are material changes in the business. Supervisory authorities, including the Ministry of Economy, assess the adequacy of the EWRA during inspections and regulatory reviews.

items.q: What is goAML and how do DNFBPs register?

a.text: goAML is the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit's (FIU) reporting platform used by regulated entities to submit Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and other regulatory reports. DNFBPs are required to register on the goAML platform, configure user governance, and establish internal reporting workflows to meet STR filing obligations. FinApt supports organizations through the full goAML registration process, system configuration, user governance setup, and the documentation of internal reporting protocols to ensure regulatory reporting readiness.

items.q: What are the penalties for AML/CFT non-compliance in the UAE?

a.text: The UAE imposes significant administrative and financial penalties for AML/CFT non-compliance. Under Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025, penalties can include substantial financial fines, suspension or withdrawal of operating licenses, public censure, and in serious cases criminal prosecution of responsible individuals. Supervisory authorities — including the Ministry of Economy, CBUAE, SCA, DFSA, and ADGM — actively monitor and enforce compliance, and have demonstrated increasing willingness to impose formal sanctions on non-compliant entities.

items.q: What is the difference between Customer Due Diligence (CDD) and Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD)?

a.text: Customer Due Diligence (CDD) is the standard level of identity verification and risk assessment applied to customers at onboarding and on an ongoing basis — including verifying identity, understanding the nature of the business relationship, and identifying the Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO). Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) is a more stringent level of scrutiny applied to higher-risk customers such as Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs), customers in high-risk jurisdictions, or those presenting elevated transaction risk profiles. EDD requires additional documentation, senior management approval, and more frequent monitoring.

items.q: What is a Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) and when must it be filed?

a.text: A Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) is a mandatory report filed with the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) via the goAML system when a regulated entity suspects that a transaction or attempted transaction may be linked to money laundering, terrorist financing, or proliferation financing. DNFBPs are required to file STRs promptly upon forming a suspicion — there is no de minimis threshold. Filing must be accompanied by proper internal documentation of the suspicion and the decision-making process.

items.q: Can a DNFBP outsource its Compliance Officer or MLRO function in the UAE?

a.text: Yes. DNFBPs in the UAE may engage external compliance professionals or firms to provide outsourced Compliance Officer or Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) services, subject to regulatory requirements regarding accountability and oversight. The outsourced function must include program oversight, regulatory liaison, monitoring of obligations, management reporting, and continuous risk assessment review. Outsourcing does not transfer regulatory responsibility — the entity remains accountable for compliance outcomes. FinApt provides structured outsourced compliance leadership support designed specifically for DNFBPs.

Understanding Company Liquidation: A Comprehensive Guide

Company liquidation is a formal process in which a business ceases operations, and its assets are sold off to pay creditors. In the context of business closure, understanding company liquidation is crucial for ensuring a smooth and compliant transition.
Types of Company Liquidation
There are different types of company liquidation , each tailored to specific circumstances. The two primary types are:

items: Voluntary Liquidation: This occurs when a company’s shareholders decide to voluntarily close the business, often due to financial difficulties or strategic decisions. Voluntary liquidation can be further divided into creditors’ voluntary liquidation (when the company is insolvent) and members’ voluntary liquidation (when the company is solvent but the shareholders wish to wind it up).

Compulsory Liquidation: This type of liquidation is initiated by a court order, often at the request of creditors who seek to recover outstanding debts. In this case, the court appoints a liquidator to oversee the process and ensure that all assets are liquidated to pay off debts.

Debt Settlement: The liquidator uses the proceeds from the asset sale to pay off the company’s debts. Creditors are paid in a specific order, with secured creditors typically having priority.
Final Distribution: After settling all debts, any remaining funds are distributed to the shareholders or other entitled parties.
Legal Dissolution: The final step in company liquidation is the legal dissolution of the company, effectively removing it from the register of companies and ceasing its existence as a legal entity.

Strategic Business Decisions: Sometimes, companies opt for voluntary liquidation as part of a strategic business decision. This may occur when a business has fulfilled its purpose, when the owners wish to retire, or when they want to exit the market while the company is still solvent.
Legal Compulsion: In cases where a company fails to comply with legal obligations or faces significant lawsuits, compulsory liquidation may be enforced by a court.

By uncovering and resolving these discrepancies, the liquidation audit ensures that the company’s financial status is accurately reflected, which is crucial for fair asset distribution and compliance.

Common Questions About Transaction Due Diligence
Answers to the questions we hear most from acquirers, investors, and sellers across the UAE, KSA, and Cyprus.

items.q: What is Transaction Due Diligence and why is it important?

a.text: Transaction due diligence is a structured investigation conducted before completing an M&A deal, investment, or capital raise. It covers the financial, tax, commercial, legal, and operational dimensions of a target business. It is important because it enables buyers, investors, and sellers to understand true risks and value drivers — preventing costly surprises post-close and enabling more informed deal pricing, structuring, and negotiation.

items.q: How long does a due diligence engagement typically take?

a.text: The timeline depends on the scope and complexity of the transaction. A focused financial due diligence on a mid-market business typically takes three to five weeks. Broader multi-workstream engagements — covering financial, tax, commercial, legal, and operational streams simultaneously — can take six to ten weeks. At FinApt, we align our timelines to deal deadlines and can mobilise quickly for time-sensitive processes.

items.q: What is the difference between buy-side and sell-side due diligence?

a.text: Buy-side due diligence is commissioned by the acquirer or investor to evaluate the target before signing. Sell-side due diligence (also called Vendor Due Diligence or VDD) is commissioned by the seller to prepare for the sale process. VDD gives sellers early visibility into potential buyer concerns, helps resolve issues pre-market, and enables a more controlled and efficient process — ultimately supporting better valuation and deal certainty.

items.q: Why is Financial Due Diligence critical even when audited accounts are available?

a.text: Audited accounts confirm compliance with accounting standards — but they are not designed to assess deal-specific risk. Financial due diligence goes further: it analyses the quality and sustainability of earnings, normalises EBITDA for non-recurring items, assesses working capital trends, and identifies off-balance-sheet liabilities. These insights directly affect deal pricing, SPA terms, and post-close adjustments — none of which an audit is structured to address.

items.q: Can FinApt handle multi-jurisdiction due diligence across UAE, KSA, and other markets?

a.text: Yes. FinApt operates across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Cyprus, and has experience managing multi-jurisdictional due diligence mandates. Our team understands the regulatory, tax, and commercial nuances of each market. For engagements spanning additional geographies, we coordinate with trusted local specialists while maintaining a single, integrated view of deal risk for our clients.

items.q: What types of transactions does FinApt support with due diligence?

a.text: We support a broad range of transactions including mergers and acquisitions, private equity investments, management buyouts, minority stake acquisitions, joint ventures, and pre-IPO processes. We also assist businesses preparing for capital raises or strategic partnerships where a credible, independent view of the business is essential for counterparty confidence.

items.q: How does Tax Due Diligence protect deal value?

a.text: Tax exposures — including unreported liabilities, transfer pricing issues, and compliance gaps — can significantly reduce a deal's value or create post-close obligations that were not priced into the transaction. Tax due diligence identifies these exposures before signing, giving buyers leverage to seek price adjustments, indemnities, or escrow arrangements. For sellers, early tax review allows issues to be resolved before they become deal-breakers.

items.q: When should a seller commission Vendor Due Diligence?

a.text: Ideally, VDD should be commissioned three to six months before going to market. This allows sufficient time to identify and resolve financial, tax, or operational issues before they are discovered by buyers. Early preparation also enables better data room organisation, cleaner management accounts, and a stronger negotiating position. Sellers who invest in VDD typically experience smoother processes, fewer re-trades, and stronger final valuations.

One of the most immediate penalties businesses face for non-compliance with corporate tax regulations is a financial fine for failing to register on time. According to the Federal Tax Authority (FTA) , businesses that meet the taxable income threshold must complete their corporate tax registration within the specified deadlines. Failure to do so can result in substantial penalties that increase over time.

Additionally, late or inaccurate corporate tax filings can also lead to penalties. These fines can accumulate rapidly and severely impact your company’s bottom line. The FTA imposes fines for both late submissions and errors in tax returns, which can also trigger audits and further scrutiny from the authorities.
Common penalties include:

items: Failure to register for corporate tax : Fines that escalate based on the delay.

Businesses that fail to meet their corporate tax payment obligations in full and on time may be subject to interest on the unpaid amount. This interest is typically calculated from the due date of the payment until the date the outstanding tax is paid in full.

In addition to interest, continued failure to meet tax payment deadlines can result in more severe penalties, further increasing the financial burden on your company. Unpaid taxes, combined with accumulating interest, can strain cash flow and negatively affect your company’s financial stability.

items.q: What is the corporate tax rate in the UAE?

a.text: The standard corporate tax rate in the UAE is set at 9% on taxable income exceeding AED 375,000. Businesses earning less than this threshold are typically exempt from corporate tax, but they are still required to file returns and report income in compliance with Federal Tax Authority (FTA) regulations. Certain free zone entities may also be subject to different rules, depending on the nature of their activities and their compliance with the UAE Corporate Tax Law .
This rate is considered competitive globally and is part of the UAE’s effort to align with international taxation standards while maintaining its reputation as a business-friendly environment.

items.q: Who is required to register for corporate tax in the UAE?

a.text: All businesses operating in the UAE , including mainland companies , free zone entities , and multinational corporations, that exceed the taxable income threshold of AED 375,000 must register for corporate tax . Even businesses that expect to fall below this threshold are encouraged to register with the Federal Tax Authority (FTA) to ensure full compliance with UAE laws.

Companies engaged in the extraction of natural resources are subject to a separate tax regime and may be exempt from the general corporate tax. Entities based in free zones that meet specific economic substance criteria may also benefit from tax incentives, though they are still required to comply with reporting requirements.

items.q: What documents are required for corporate tax registration?

a.text: The corporate tax registration process with the Federal Tax Authority (FTA) requires businesses to provide several essential documents. These include:

items: Trade license : Proof of your company’s legal registration in the UAE.

Financial statements : To demonstrate taxable income and business activity in the UAE.

items.q: What are the deadlines for corporate tax filing in the UAE?

items.q: What is Transaction Due Diligence and why is it important?

a.text: Transaction due diligence is a structured investigation conducted before completing an M&A deal, investment, or capital raise. items.q: What is the difference between buy-side and sell-side due diligence?

a.text: Buy-side due diligence is commissioned by the acquirer or investor to evaluate the target before signing. Sell-side due diligence (also called Vendor Due Diligence or VDD) is commissioned by the seller to prepare for the sale process. a.text: Audited accounts confirm compliance with accounting standards — but they are not designed to assess deal-specific risk. Financial due diligence goes further: it analyses the quality and sustainability of earnings, normalises EBITDA for non-recurring items, assesses working capital trends, and identifies off-balance-sheet liabilities. These insights directly affect deal pricing, SPA terms, and post-close adjustments — none of which an audit is structured to address.

items.q: What is UBO disclosure and who is required to comply in the UAE?

a.text: Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) disclosure requires UAE companies to identify and register individuals who ultimately own or control 25% or more of the entity's shares or voting rights. items.q: What is Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) and does it apply to us?

Frequently Asked Questions on Valuation & Modelling
Answers to common questions on valuation and financial modelling, covering purpose, methodology, compliance, and practical application across transactions and reporting.

items.q: What is business valuation used for?

a.text: Business valuation is used for transactions, financial reporting, capital raising, shareholder matters, and regulatory or legal purposes. It helps stakeholders make informed decisions based on defensible financial analysis.

items.q: When is purchase price allocation (PPA) required?

a.text: Purchase price allocation is required following a business acquisition under IFRS 3 to allocate the transaction consideration to identifiable tangible and intangible assets and liabilities.

items.q: How does impairment testing work?

a.text: Impairment testing assesses whether the carrying value of goodwill or intangible assets exceeds their recoverable amount, in accordance with IAS 36, using cash flow projections and appropriate discount rates.

items.q: How do you choose the right valuation method?

a.text: The valuation method depends on the purpose of the valuation, the nature of the business, data availability, and stakeholder expectations. Approaches such as DCF, market multiples, and net asset value are often used together for validation.

items.q: Can valuation outcomes be defended during audit or disputes?

a.text: Yes. Defensible valuations are supported by transparent assumptions, consistent methodologies, and comprehensive documentation, allowing them to withstand audit, regulatory, or litigation scrutiny.

items.q: How often should valuations or financial models be updated?

a.text: Valuations and financial models should be updated whenever there are material changes in performance, market conditions, ownership structure, or reporting requirements. Investment valuations are commonly updated quarterly or semi-annually.
